title: Hands-On Marine Biology: Jefferson University
summary: Biology students from Thomas Jefferson University traveled to Curaçao for a hands-on research experience studying endangered green sea turtles and hawksbill turtles.
body:
Biology students from Thomas Jefferson University, Philadelphia, traveled to Curaçao for a hands-on research experience studying endangered green sea turtles and hawksbill turtles in their natural environment.

Led by Dr. Manuela Tripepi and supported by Dr. Jeff Ashley, students participated in real-world conservation research, including turtle netting and tagging, habitat analysis, seagrass sampling, and nest monitoring. Over the course of the trip, students applied classroom theory to fieldwork, gaining direct experience in marine biology, wildlife conservation, and data collection methods used by professional researchers.

This short-term study abroad experience exposed students to a new culture, a new ecosystem, and the realities of conservation science. From releasing turtles back into the ocean to tracking previously tagged individuals, each moment reinforced the importance of protecting marine habitats and endangered species.

At Jefferson, experiential learning is central to how students learn. Opportunities like this allow students to grow as scientists, conservationists, and global citizens by engaging directly with the world they are studying.

title: STCC at the third United Nations Ocean Conference
summary: Sea Turtle Conservation Curaçao participated in the third United Nations Ocean Conference, sharing our conservation efforts on the global stage.
body:
Sea Turtle Conservation Curaçao is proud to have participated in the third United Nations Ocean Conference, representing our small island nation on the global stage in the fight to protect our oceans and marine wildlife.

The conference brought together world leaders, scientists, conservationists, and stakeholders from around the globe to address the critical challenges facing our oceans. For STCC, this was an invaluable opportunity to share our work, learn from others, and strengthen international partnerships.

Why This Matters

Sea turtles are a shared resource – they migrate across international boundaries and face threats throughout their range. Protecting them requires international cooperation and coordinated efforts.

At the conference, we had the opportunity to:

  • Share our research on Fibropapillomatosis and Curaçao's unique role as a global hotspot
  • Connect with other Caribbean conservation organizations
  • Learn about innovative conservation techniques being used worldwide
  • Advocate for stronger protections for sea turtles and marine habitats

Looking Forward

Participating in events like the UN Ocean Conference helps raise awareness of the conservation challenges we face in Curaçao and reinforces our commitment to being part of the global solution.

We returned with new ideas, new connections, and renewed determination to protect the sea turtles that call our waters home.

Thank you to all our supporters who make this work possible. Together, we can create a better future for sea turtles and our oceans.

title: Educational video about Green sea turtles
summary: We're excited to share our new educational video about Green sea turtles, designed to help people learn about these amazing creatures.
body:
We're excited to announce the release of our new educational video about Green sea turtles! This video is part of our ongoing mission to spread awareness about sea turtle conservation and inspire people to protect these incredible creatures.

About the Video

The video covers everything you need to know about Green sea turtles, including:

  • Physical characteristics and how to identify them
  • Diet and feeding behavior
  • Life cycle from egg to adult
  • Habitat and migration patterns
  • Threats they face in Curaçao and worldwide
  • How everyone can help protect them

Why Green Sea Turtles?

Green sea turtles are the most commonly seen species in Curaçao's waters, making them an excellent starting point for learning about sea turtle conservation. Despite their name, Green turtles are actually named for the green color of their body fat, not their shells!

As adults, Green sea turtles are primarily herbivores, feeding on seagrasses and algae. This makes them important "gardeners" of the sea – their grazing helps keep seagrass beds healthy, which in turn provides habitat for countless other marine species.

Education is Key

At STCC, we believe that education is fundamental to conservation. When people understand the amazing lives of sea turtles and the challenges they face, they're more likely to take action to protect them.

This video is designed for viewers of all ages and can be used in schools, community groups, and at home. We encourage teachers and parents to share it widely!

Watch and Share

The video is available on our social media channels. Please watch, like, and share it with your friends and family. Every view helps spread the message of sea turtle conservation!

Follow us on Instagram and Facebook to watch the video and stay updated on our latest educational content.

title: Release hatchling at Blue Bay
summary: A wonderful moment as we released hatchlings at Blue Bay. These tiny turtles are now on their journey in the ocean.
body:
What a magical morning at Blue Bay! We had the privilege of releasing sea turtle hatchlings into the ocean, watching as these tiny creatures began their incredible journey into the Caribbean Sea.

The Moment of Release

There's nothing quite like watching baby sea turtles make their first steps toward the ocean. These tiny hatchlings, each no bigger than the palm of your hand, instinctively know to head toward the water, guided by the light reflecting off the sea.

As they scrambled across the sand and entered the waves, we were reminded why we do this work. Each hatchling represents hope for the future of sea turtles in Curaçao.

Why Hatchling Releases Matter

Sea turtle hatchlings face incredible odds. It's estimated that only about 1 in 1,000 hatchlings will survive to adulthood. They face threats from predators, plastic pollution, and many other dangers during their "lost years" in the open ocean.

By monitoring nests and ensuring hatchlings have a safe path to the sea, we help give them the best possible start in life. Every hatchling that makes it to the water is a small victory for conservation.

Nesting Season in Curaçao

Nesting season in Curaçao runs from approximately June through December. During this time, female sea turtles come ashore at night to lay their eggs in nests dug in the sand. After about 60 days of incubation, the hatchlings emerge – usually at night – and make their way to the sea.

Our volunteers monitor known nesting beaches during this season, documenting nesting activity and protecting nests from disturbance. When hatchlings emerge, we sometimes assist with releases to ensure they reach the water safely.

Thank You

Thank you to everyone who supports our work. Moments like these remind us why sea turtle conservation matters. These hatchlings are now out there in the ocean, and hopefully, some of them will one day return to Curaçao's beaches to nest – continuing the cycle of life that has existed for millions of years.

Want to help protect sea turtle nests? Consider volunteering with us during nesting season!

title: Rescue at Kokomobeach
summary: STCC responded to an emergency call to rescue a turtle entangled in fishing lines and infected with FP tumors at Kokomo beach.
body:
Friday the 20th of October, STCC got an emergency call from the captain of the boat La Menta Boat Trips. They picked up a turtle in open water entangled in fishing lines and infected with FP tumors. They were on their way to Kokomo beach.

A STCC rescue team was formed and the turtle was handed over. After a quick examination the turtle was brought to the vet for further examination.

Thanks to Kokomo Beach Curaçao, Soul Divers, La Menta Boat Trips, and other volunteers for their help.

This turtle is number 147 this year. We keep you posted on how this green turtle is recovering in the future.

If you want to help us with the treatment of this and other turtles, please consider making a donation to support our rescue and rehabilitation work.

title: Unlocking the Secrets of Turtles: Using transmitters to enhance conservation efforts
summary: A Paradise FM radio interview highlights STCC's research collaboration using transmitters to track turtles affected by FP disease.
body:
Paradise FM's radio interview with Ard Vreugdenhil highlights a unique research collaboration between Sea Turtle Conservation Curaçao (STCC) and Dr. Manuela Tripepi, Associate Professor of Biology at Jefferson University. Focusing on turtles affected by FP disease, the project utilizes transmitters to pinpoint their specific feeding areas. Volunteers and divers play a vital role in gathering data for conservation efforts.

The transmitter research project is led by Ard Vreugdenhil in partnership with Dr. Manuela Tripepi. The project's primary objective is to identify precise feeding areas for turtles carrying FP disease. Identifying specific feeding areas is crucial for targeted conservation measures.

Ard Vreugdenhil acknowledges challenges for the FP turtles but remains optimistic, highlighting the increased awareness of the disease.

Paradise FM's interview with Ard Vreugdenhil reveals a promising collaboration studying turtles with FP disease. Utilizing transmitters and the dedication of volunteers, the project sheds light on feeding areas, benefiting scientific knowledge and conservation efforts.

title: Unveiling the feeding grounds of Curaçao Sea Turtles: A Collaborative Project in Tagging and Tracking
summary: A collaborative project between Dr. Manuela Tripepi and STCC uses radio transmitters to tag and track sea turtles, revealing their feeding habits.
body:
Sea turtles glide gracefully through the depths, as they reach the coastal waters of Curaçao. It is here that they like to spend some time before they continue their journey onward. Unlocking the mysteries of their feeding habits is essential for their conservation. Enter a unique collaboration between Dr. Manuela Tripepi, Associate Professor of Biology at Jefferson University, Philadelphia, and Sea Turtle Conservation Curaçao. Together, they embark on a project to tag and track sea turtles in Curaçao, shedding light on their elusive behaviors and contributing to their long-term protection.

Sea turtles are remarkable creatures, and their feeding habits play a crucial role in maintaining the health of marine ecosystems. Their foraging behaviors and preferred feeding grounds could be factors to the Fibropapillomatosis (FP) disease currently found on the green sea turtles present around the island.

The pathogenesis and epidemiology of FP in marine sea turtles is poorly understood, though the disease is believed to be caused by a combination of factors that activate the Chelonid alphaherpesvirus 5 (ChHV5), which is responsible for the disease. One primary factor is believed to be the environmental pollutants present in the turtles' habitats and a compromised immune system in the turtles. In Curaçao, FP has been observed in green sea turtle populations in specific areas and is considered a major threat to the species' survival.

Using radio transmitters, this project will collect data on affected sea turtles and compare their habits with healthy ones living in the same areas. The project will first analyze the area of Caracas Baai, where 75% of the turtles examined showed tumors.

Dr. Manuela Tripepi brings her expertise and passion for research that focuses on stress responses. Her research investigates how different organisms respond to various stressors and the impact that these stressors can have on their survival strategies. Working in close collaboration, the team will carefully capture, tag, and release the sea turtles while ensuring the safety and well-being of these magnificent creatures.

Once tagged, sea turtles become living data transmitters. Their movements are tracked using radio transmitter technology, allowing the researchers to map their migration patterns, identify feeding spots, and explore the impact of environmental factors on their behavior. Understanding their feeding habits and migratory patterns enables the identification and protection of critical habitats. It empowers policymakers and conservation organizations to implement targeted measures to preserve these habitats and mitigate human-induced threats.

Dr. Manuela Tripepi and Sea Turtle Conservation Curaçao combine scientific expertise and fieldwork experience that together with radio technology will make this project a success. This endeavor not only advances our knowledge but also lays the foundation for effective conservation strategies. Together, we can ensure the future of these enchanting creatures and the fragile ecosystems they call home.

title: STCC Rescue Mission at Playa Piskado!
summary: Our team carried out a successful rescue mission at Playa Piskado, removing a fishing hook from a young green turtle.
body:
We are happy to share the news of a successful rescue mission carried out by our dedicated team from Sea Turtle Conservation Curaçao!

Our intern Ingo spotted a young green turtle with a hook in its beak. Together with Ard, our STCC field coordinator, they located the green turtle and brought it to shore. Here they removed the embedded fishing hook, relieving the sea turtle of its pain.

After a health check-up, the turtle was released safely.

This rescue serves as a powerful reminder of the impact we have on marine life and the importance of protecting our turtles. Together, we can make a difference!

title: Sambil Chi Chi painting on World Sea Turtle Day
summary: STCC and Chi Chi Curaçao hosted an amazing paint event at Sambil on World Sea Turtle Day, combining art, conservation, and fun.
body:
On June 16, 2023 – World Sea Turtle Day – we had an amazing paint event in Sambil with Chi Chi Curaçao and STCC. It was an unforgettable experience that combined art, conservation, and a whole lot of fun. There was a lot of enthusiasm and positive energy.

The purpose of the event was to let visitors paint their own Chi Chi turtle. These iconic and colorful figures are a true symbol of Curaçao. It also raised some funds for STCC to continue our work.

In the meantime, visitors learned about the efforts made to protect and preserve the sea turtles. It was great to see young kids painting a Chi Chi turtle. They will be our future ambassadors.

A big thanks to the public helping paint, the volunteers, Chi Chi Curaçao, and everyone involved in making this event a huge success!

title: Sea turtle nesting season 2023
summary: Exciting discoveries during beach patrols as volunteers found multiple turtle nests, including at least 4 confirmed hawksbill turtle nests.
body:
Discoveries at Curaçao beaches!

The last weeks our volunteers were fortunate to discover a lot of tracks during their beach patrols. They followed the tracks that led to some turtle nests. At least 4 nests are confirmed hawksbill turtles. Also a few attempts were discovered.

It's so wonderful to witness these wonders of nature. The volunteers did everything to protect these nests and put markers. They also filled all the forms for the necessary documentation STCC uses for scientific research.

We hope these mothers come back for more nesting, and in 2 months we hope they all hatch safely.

title: Field education with Carmabi rangers
summary: STCC volunteers and field coordinator Ard trained Carmabi rangers in turtle conservation fieldwork at Boca Ascencion.
body:
Training Carmabi rangers at Boca Ascencion

Fieldwork and education constitute fundamental pillars for STCC. Engaging young people in fieldwork activities imparts knowledge while nurturing curiosity, fostering personal growth, and igniting environmental passion.

On February 4, 2023, three volunteers (Chris, Whitney, and Henk) and field coordinator Ard conducted training for Carmabi rangers, teaching foundational field activities in turtle conservation.

Training activities included:

  • Rescuing stranded turtles
  • Locating nests
  • Finding nests using recorded coordinates

The ranger groups participated enthusiastically in three training sessions, gaining substantial knowledge about turtles during the Saturday morning event. Fieldwork enables young people to move beyond classroom walls and explore the real world.

title: Release hatchlings at Kokomo
summary: About 50 hatchlings from a nest at San Juan were released at Kokomo beach at sunset, giving them the best chance at survival.
body:
Friday the 25th of November 2022, a nest at San Juan hatched, but there were still about 50 hatchlings left in the nest that did not come out. In order to ensure better survival chances for this lot, our volunteers and field coordinator planned the release on the very next sunset.

The San Juan area unfortunately closes before sunset, therefore an accessible and open location was needed and Kokomo provided the best option for these babies to crawl into the big wide sea.

One of our volunteers, Gavin O'Neill, made wonderful photographs of this evening capturing the magic of these tiny turtles making their way to the ocean.

title: Blue Bay 2022 nesting and hatching recap
summary: During the 2022 nesting season, volunteers helped a hawksbill turtle missing a back flipper successfully nest at Blue Bay, resulting in 5 nests.
body:
During the nesting season in 2022, a female Hawksbill turtle visited the coastline of Blue Bay to lay her eggs. During this process one of our volunteers spotted the female turtle as she was making an attempt to dig a nest. Thanks to the recorded data of the previous year, it was possible to estimate where and approximately when she would make her attempts.

This particular turtle had a disadvantage – she was missing a back flipper. It would be very difficult for her to lay her eggs and probably it would lead to failed attempts and ultimately no nests. Thanks to the dedication of our volunteers and our field coordinator, we succeeded to help the turtle dig her nest till she was satisfied to release her eggs.

These eggs have been relocated to a better location in the same bay and now we have 5 nests to look forward to. These are achievements to celebrate. Thank you to everyone involved in making this happen!

Watch the hatching at Blue Bay video on YouTube.
